platforms.title: Gastritis: Why Does Your Stomach Lining Keep Breaking Down?
platforms.meta_description: Gastritis isn't only about spicy food. Caffeine, regular painkiller use, and salty meals can each wear down your stomach's protective lining in different ways.
platforms.body_html:
Spicy food gets blamed for gastritis more than almost anything else, but the stomach lining's ability to defend itself matters just as much as what you eat on any given day. When that lining thins, the same amount of acid that was fine last month can suddenly cause burning and pain, sometimes with no obvious change in diet at all. Three everyday habits — coffee, regular painkiller use, and salty food — each wear down that defense through a completely different mechanism, which is why the fix for one rarely helps with another.

Three Ways the Stomach's Defense Gets Worn Down

The stomach makes strong acid without digesting itself because a mucus-and-bicarbonate layer protects the lining underneath. Coffee interferes with that balance from the acid side: research published in PNAS found that caffeine directly stimulates acid-producing cells in the stomach through a bitter-taste receptor pathway, triggering the release of gastrin, the hormone that signals the stomach to produce more acid.

Regular use of over-the-counter painkillers like ibuprofen works on the defense side instead. According to a review in the journal Gastroenterology, these drugs block prostaglandins, compounds that normally keep the protective mucus and bicarbonate layer intact and maintain blood flow to the stomach lining. Researchers describe gastric injury from these drugs as needing both the direct acidic irritation and this loss of prostaglandin protection together — which is why occasional use rarely causes problems, but daily use over weeks or months often does.

Salty food adds a third pressure. A high-salt diet damages gastric mucosal cells through osmotic stress and makes it easier for Helicobacter pylori bacteria to colonize the stomach lining, according to research published in the journal Infection and Immunity. Over years, this combination is linked to atrophic gastritis, a thinning of the stomach lining that raises long-term risk — the effect is strongest with sustained high intake rather than one salty meal.

What Actually Happens When You Fix These Three Habits

  • Drink coffee with food, not on an empty stomach — food buffers the extra acid caffeine triggers, and keeping intake to a moderate amount reduces the ongoing stimulus.
  • Use painkillers at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time — for pain lasting more than a few days, ask a doctor or pharmacist about options that are gentler on the stomach lining.
  • Cut back on broths, pickled sides, and other very salty foods — choosing lower-sodium preparations most days matters more than avoiding salt entirely once.
  • Avoid mixing painkillers with alcohol — alcohol irritates the same stomach lining that prostaglandins normally protect, so combining the two multiplies the risk beyond what either one causes alone.

If you remember one thing, it's this: gastritis symptoms usually ease within days to weeks once the habit driving them is dialed back, since the stomach lining regenerates quickly on its own. That said, black or tarry stools, vomiting blood, or pain that persists beyond two weeks despite these changes are signs to see a doctor rather than wait it out — they can point to a bleeding ulcer. This article is for general information only and isn't medical advice.
